Research on human population history has long used models of population splitting with subsequent admixture to make sense of polymorphism data (mostly from humans, but also from commensal species). In this paper, Maier et al use introduce algorithmic improvements that allow them to search the space of such "admixture graphs" more exhaustively and use them to re-evaluate a large number of published results in order to investigate whether the corresponding studies really found the "best" models. They find that they generally did not, and conclude that greater caution is in order when interpreting these kinds of data.

The work is encyclopedic (the single-spaced manuscript is over 50 pages - a monograph, really) and well written. The conclusions are well supported and illustrated by many examples.

The main problem I have with the paper is that reading it feels a bit like entering a cladistics meeting where people debate things like the significance of a particular scale on the middle toe of the Lesser Two-headed Tree Wrangler. While the overall point is clear, the details (and there are many) will be obscure unless you are intimately familiar with the specific examples. This means that the majority of the contents of the paper will/must be skipped by those not directly working on human population history. Which is a pity, as the overall conclusions are generally relevant.

Furthermore, just as would have been the case at a cladistics meeting, this paper is narrowly focused on a particular analysis framework. Technical terms like "f-statistic" are thrown around without introduction. In the few remaining corners of population genetics that do not work on human genetics, there are those who do not think in terms of discrete populations, and who hold heretical notions about isolation-by-distance. The question of whether *any* admixture graph is a good model for the data is not asked here - and it arguably should be given the generality of the title. As the paper makes very clear, there are indeed limits to what we can infer about history from genetic data. However, beyond a vague "here be monsters", the paper offers a general audience little guidance about which of the large numbers of claims in illustrious journals are actually likely to be true.

I think this is an excellent and important paper written for a narrow audience. If you want to reach a larger audience, a very different paper is in order.

I also think you do not address the very broad question in the title – this would again be a different paper.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors aim to correct inference problems with existing software by changing and implementing new features of Admixtools. The conclusions are supported by the results. The program will likely be much used.

The authors deserve credit for acknowledging that there might be many admixture graphs fitting a given data set equally well and that this fact has not been acknowledged in any/many previous study(ies), incl the authors own :-

Also they deserve credit for a quite substantial re-analysis of already published data.

The novelty and selling point seem to be a new version of Admixturetools (together with re-analysis). However, several of the "new ideas" implemented are already in Admixturetools 7.0.2, so the novelty is quite limited. While I acknowledge computational speed-ups, clever data manipulations, proper testing and so forth are important and important to publish, it does not seem to have the novelty-level required for eLife.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors briefly describe improvements to the popular ADMIXTOOLS software, now released as ADMIXTOOLS2. These include computational speedups that allow computationally-intensive resampling-based methods such as bootstrap to help assess model fit, even for large datasets, as well as a more extensive automated search over model space (exhaustive search is still infeasible, so constraints based on judgments of plausibility are still required).

Using these improved tools, the authors extensively re-analyse 8 published datasets (human, dog and horse), and find many conclusions of the original authors about demographic history to be not well supported. This is because there exist other plausible models, often many of them, that fit the data better, sometimes significantly so, that does not support the original authors' conclusions based on their preferred model. Often there are also even more alternative models that fit the data worse than the published model, but not significantly worse and so they cannot be excluded.

I'm a statistical methods person not closely familiar with any of the studies re-analysed here, so I don't have deep insights about the revised analyses proposed here. However, the authors seem to me to have conducted a careful and well-justified model fitting exercise with important conclusions and implications for future analyses.

The authors conclude with recommendations for future analyses of genetic data to make inferences about population history. They hope to change the field in a similar way to the step change in standards for statistical significance in association studies that occurred around 2008. The guidelines proposed are no doubt open to improvement over time, but I agree that this study is likely to have a big impact on the field of demographic history inference leading to better-justified conclusions from future analyses. The problem addressed is much more complex than genetic association, and conclusions based on limited exploration of a vast model space will always open to further improvement.

It's a very good paper, I don't have much to say at a general level except that it is very long and perhaps trying to do too much. The introduction of ADMIXTOOLS2 and the general discussion about principles of model fitting both seem inadequate. In contrast, the discussion of the re-analyses of datasets is very thorough. Perhaps two papers would have been better?

In a generally well-written paper I found the first sentence of the abstract confusing "… the only information needed to capture the patterns of allele frequency correlation among populations". Why is "capturing.… correlation" your primary focus? I would restate with an objective that is comprehensible to a general reader.

Abstract L17: "Our results suggest that strong claims.…. be made when all well-fitting and temporally plausible models share common topological features" This doesn't follow from the results, you are asserting it as a principle. The "all.… models" is perhaps a strong requirement when there are many of them.

L42 " finding fitting".

L163 " the time required to process.. trivial compared to the time required to compute.…" I found this confusing because its unclear to me what "process" means here.

L291 " Parameters with extremely wide confidence intervals can thus be immediately shown to be poorly determined." Vacuous statement – the paper is already very long! Delete.

L300 define "worst-residual" (maybe refer here to an explanation in methods).

L303 "… methods relying on AIC or BIC.… were over-aggressive". The merits of resampling based versus likelihood based model comparison is an extremely important topic, it's beyond the scope of the present paper to discuss fully here but you should be able to cite some authorities to support this claim.

L342 "to test the null hypothesis that the true difference in log-likelihood.… is zero" The log-likelihood is a function of the data so is not appropriate in a null hypothesis, which should be a statement about models/parameters and not data.

L375 "… without either fixing one of them or forcing the lengths to be evenly distributed." not strictly true and there must be a better way to say what you mean: we can only estimate 1 parameter, not both.

L514 "Lower scores of the fits obtained.… indicate overfitting to the full data set." This is one of the first of many references to overfitting that I found unsatisfactory as I did not notice a discussion of its implications for your analyses. Overfitting is a broad and ubiquitous phenomenon, why is it important here? I feel you should remove these (not needed to justify your main conclusions) or explain better. Are you diagnosing a mechanism that has led other authors astray? Also the specific wording "overfitting to the full data set" seems odd, is there any other kind of overfitting?

L614 "Near East" Near to what? East of what? Please use standard terminology that is meaningful to a general reader, not this outdated colonial-era relic. Similarly for "Middle East" (L687): that term is widely used but not appropriate in a science paper, use "West Asia" or "Eastern Mediterranean" something more specific. Also "Levantine" – is that a standard term in the dog world? It seems not from a quick search. Replace with some more meaningful to a general reader.

L662 "pseudo-diploid" has not been explained. I looked it up and the meaning I found doesn't make sense here.

L1119 "cannot be right" is not an appropriate way to summarise statistical evidence.

L1505 explain(or replace) "high degeneracy".

L1677 "time and population size as the two sources of genetic drift" they are factors affecting rather than sources.

Reviewer #4: (Recommendations for the authors):

Overview:

The article is composed of a review of the existing method for the admixture graph estimation and the update of the ADMIXTURETOOLS, and the application of the package to real-life examples. The Results section is hard to follow, and it contains substantial parts which would better fit the Introduction section and the User Manual. Figures are in their draft versions.

Plusses:

The existing ADMIXTURETOOLS method was improved by useful features (confidence intervals and identifiability of admixture graph parameters and the searching the space of all admixture graphs), and heuristics significantly sped it up for f-statistics computations.

Minuses:

L139: what are the philosophical differences between two versions of ADMIXTURETOOLS.

L169: the bias should be demonstrated more clearly.

L175: what is the regression approach to estimate f-statistics.

L186: "pseudo-diploid and pseudo-haploid" – these computational details are not properly explained if they are essential.

L190: "unbiased" – analysis of bias based on the number of samples is required.

L194: "inbreed: YES" option – user manual detail. This detail does not mean much for users who have not worked with ADMIXTURETOOLS.

L201: "incorrect algorithm for calculating" – should be explained more. It would be more important than to mention user manual details.

Figure1 should be rearranged in columns; there are a lot of places for it.

Figure1a: low subfigure x-axis should be reorganized.

Figure1b: if the formula for the F4 is exact, then what is the source of mentioned bias, and where is the heuristics.

Figure1c: what is the difference between all F3/4. Is there any conventional definition, and what is the difference between mentioned definitions? This should be organized as a table, nut a subfigure.

Figure1d: Why are formulas for F3 not presented.

Figure2: Dash dots for the y-axis levels should be presented to compare bars.

Figure3: (a,b) – what does it mean? The figure is in the draft stage.

1. No basic explanation for unprepared readers, what are f2/f3/f4, and what is the practical difference between them.

2. The article contains many references to features from the ADMIXTURETOOLS by names, without explanation. Authors should provide the text to a broad audience of eLife, but not for the users of ADMIXTURETOOLS.

Suggestions:

1. I strongly recommend revising the manuscript stricture. For example, the result section is a blend of "literature revie,"&"draft result"&"methods"&"program manual".

2. The text should be significantly reduced, especially when it is hard to read and seems to be in its draft version.

3. Type of the article should be defined more clearer: whether it is a research article? New method? Or a review manuscript of the existing methods.

4. Be more accurate with figures. In the current version, figures are not properly arranged and resemble draft versions.

5. Introduce the abbreviation for "admixture graph" as, for instance, AG.

results.result: Simulation studies demonstrate that even for relatively simple admixture graphs (8-9 populations, 4-5 admixture events), the findGraphs method frequently identifies alternative models that fit nominally or significantly better than the true topology, with high topological diversity among well-fitting models.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 and C43-C45 are directly supported by simulation data presented in Figure 1, showing that 60-100% of simulated datasets had at least one AG fitting significantly better than the true model depending on parsimony constraints. The high topological diversity is demonstrated visually in Figure 1e and quantitatively described in the text.

results.result: Re-analysis of 22 published admixture graphs from 8 studies revealed that for 19 out of 22 cases, alternative models with equal or better fit were identified, with many showing qualitatively different topological features regarding population history inferences.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 and C155 are strongly supported by comprehensive re-analysis data presented in Table 1, Figure 2, and detailed case studies. The systematic application of findGraphs to published datasets with bootstrap model comparison provides robust evidence for the existence of alternative well-fitting models.

results.result: Re-analysis of the Bergström et al. 2020 dog population history study identified an alternative model that fits nominally better and shows greater congruence with human population history, suggesting that parsimony constraints in the original exhaustive search may have missed the true topology.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C62 are supported by the re-analysis data (Figure 3a, Table 1) showing a nominally better-fitting alternative model (p=0.332). The parallel between the alternative dog model and established human population history patterns (C55-C58, supported by citations) strengthens the plausibility of the alternative model, though the authors appropriately note this doesn't prove it's correct.

results.result: Re-analysis of the Lazaridis et al. 2014 European population history study found 40 alternative models fitting nominally or significantly better than the published model, though most support the core conclusion of three-way admixture in modern Europeans.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72 are supported by the re-analysis showing 40 better-fitting models out of 306 distinct graphs (C64), with some fitting significantly better (C65). While most alternatives support the three-way admixture conclusion (C66), the existence of 247 models fitting not significantly worse (C71) with topological diversity demonstrates model non-uniqueness (C72).

results.result: Re-analysis of the Shinde et al. 2019 Indus Valley study shows that under strict parsimony (3 admixture events), the published model is relatively stable, but relaxing parsimony to 4 events reveals high topological diversity, indicating that key historical conclusions depend critically on the parsimony assumption.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C87 are supported by systematic re-analysis with different parsimony constraints. With 3 admixture events, only 4 alternative topologies fit nominally better (C79), all sharing key features (C80). However, qpAdm analysis (C83) and exploration with 4 admixture events (C84-C85) reveal that the parsimony constraint is contradicted by f-statistic evidence, making the key historical conclusion (C86) dependent on an unjustified assumption (C87).

results.result: Re-analysis of the Librado et al. 2021 horse domestication study reveals that the published models with 3-5 admixture events fit the data extremely poorly (WR=23.9 SE for 3 events), and only models with 8-9 admixture events achieve acceptable fits, with many contradicting key inferences from the original study.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C97 are strongly supported by quantitative fit statistics (C91: WR=23.9 SE) and systematic exploration showing acceptable fits only with 8-9 admixture events (C92). Among 16 temporally plausible models, 13 contradict the inference about CWC-Western steppe gene flow (C94), and only 8 support the Tarpan ancestry model (C97), demonstrating instability of key conclusions.

results.result: Re-analysis of the Hajdinjak et al. 2021 Upper Paleolithic study found that 71.4% of alternative models fit nominally better and 15.7% significantly better than the published model, with none of the 32 temporally plausible alternatives supporting the key finding of gene flows from Bacho Kiro IUP to all three of Ust'-Ishim, Tianyuan, and GoyetQ116-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C106 are supported by systematic re-analysis data (Table 1, Figure 2, Figure 3c). The poor absolute fit (WR=4.8 SE, C100) and evidence of overfitting (C101) are demonstrated. Critically, manual inspection of 50 best-fitting topologies identified 32 as temporally plausible (C103), but none supported the key inference about Bacho Kiro IUP gene flows (C104), undermining a central conclusion of the original study.

results.result: Re-analysis of the Lipson et al. 2020b African population history study found high topological diversity among well-fitting models, with none of the four key AG features from the original study consistently supported across temporally plausible alternatives.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 are supported by re-analysis of 2,000 models showing 11.9% fit nominally better (C108), with evidence of overfitting (C110, Figure 2). The high topological diversity (C111, Figure 4a) and lack of consistent support for any of the four key features (C112, Table 2) demonstrate that the ancestral relationships of Shum Laka individuals remain unresolved (C113).

results.result: Re-analysis of the Wang et al. 2021 East Asian population history study found that 1,724 of 1,778 alternative models fit nominally better than the published model, with the key inference about ubiquitous Andamanese-related gene flow in East Asia not supported by f-statistic analysis alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C122 are supported by systematic re-analysis (Table 1) showing 97% of models fit nominally better and 12.6% significantly better (C116). Among temporally plausible models, only 0-2 East Asian groups showed Onge-related ancestry (C117), while 19 showed European-related gene flows (C118). The best alternative model fitting significantly better (p=0.028, C120) contradicts the key inference (C121-C122).

results.result: Re-analysis of the Sikora et al. 2019 study found that for the 'Western' graph, the direction of gene flow between Mal'ta and CHG cannot be resolved by AG analysis, with 27 of 29 plausible models supporting the opposite direction from the published model; for the 'Eastern' graph, only one of three key features was universally supported.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C138 are supported by systematic re-analysis of both graphs. For the Western graph, 27/29 plausible models support gene flow opposite to the published direction (C127), consistent with qpAdm analyses (C128). For the Eastern graph, only feature 2 was universally supported among 97 plausible models (C134), while features 3 and 1 were supported by 83/97 and 28/97 models respectively (C135-C136).

results.result: The authors developed findGraphs, a new method for automated admixture graph topology optimization that combines advantages of automated and manual approaches by allowing external information to be encoded as constraints, implemented in ADMIXTOOLS 2 with substantial performance improvements.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 and C33-C36 describe the methodological contribution, which is demonstrated through successful application to simulated and real datasets throughout the manuscript. The conceptual innovation (C28) of exploring AG space rather than finding single models (C29) is clearly implemented. Performance gains (C34-C35) and new features (C36) are stated but specific benchmarks are not provided in the main text.

results.result: The study developed bootstrap-based methods for obtaining confidence intervals and p-values for model parameters and for comparing fits between models, addressing limitations of AIC/BIC approaches where effective degrees of freedom depend on graph topology.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by the methodology described and applied throughout the manuscript (referenced in Appendix 1). The bootstrap model comparison method is used consistently to assess statistical significance of fit differences (e.g., C52, C65, C120). The limitation of AIC/BIC for AGs (C32) is a valid theoretical point supported by the topology-dependent nature of model complexity.

results.result: Admixture graphs are defined as directed acyclic bifurcating graphs with edges representing genetic drift and gene flow, fitted to f-statistics which measure allele frequency correlations between populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C5-C10 provide definitional and mathematical background that is well-established in population genetics, supported by appropriate citations (Patterson et al. 2012, Lipson 2020a, etc.). These are standard definitions in the field and form the necessary foundation for the study.

results.result: Previously published methods for finding fitting admixture graphs had three key limitations: not reliably indicating whether models are unique, not providing formal goodness-of-fit tests, and not testing statistical significance of fit differences between models.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 accurately characterize limitations of prior methods (qpGraph, TreeMix) based on the authors' analysis and are supported by the demonstration throughout the manuscript that these limitations led to overconfidence in published models. The inference is reasonable given the evidence presented in the re-analyses.

results.result: Exhaustive approaches to testing all possible admixture graphs are limited to small graphs (typically ≤6 groups, 2 admixture events) due to combinatorial explosion, and can miss important alternative models when parsimony constraints are applied or additional populations are excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 are supported by citation to existing implementations (C16), computational complexity arguments (C17), and case study evidence (C18-C19, particularly the Bergström et al. re-analysis showing how adding a population revealed a missed model with 3 admixture events).

results.result: Manual construction of admixture graphs, while able to incorporate external knowledge and human judgment, has the weakness of potentially validating user biases and missing alternative topologies that may better represent true history.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 provide a balanced assessment of manual approaches, supported by extensive citations to studies using these methods (C22). The strengths (C23-C24) and weaknesses (C25-C26) are reasonable inferences supported by the case study evidence presented in the Results section.

results.result: Some admixture events are indistinguishable with f-statistics (e.g., successive gene flows between lineages with no intervening branches), making optimal complexity class selection for topology search non-straightforward for random histories.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 describe a theoretical limitation of f-statistics that is well-established knowledge (C40) and is demonstrated in the simulation results where models with n events could be overly complex (C41-C42). This is a valid inference from the simulation data.

results.result: While admixture graphs represent a powerful conceptual framework, manual construction without automated exploration can lead to overconfidence, and the ideal outcome of identifying uniquely fitting models is almost never achieved for graphs with >8 populations and >3 admixture events.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C146 synthesize the main findings and recommendations. The inference about overconfidence (C140) is supported by the comprehensive re-analysis data. The statement about ideal outcomes rarely being achieved (C142) is supported by the authors' experience and the case studies presented. The recommendation for rigorous protocols (C146) follows logically from the findings.

results.result: The proposed guidelines for admixture graph analysis are analogous to protocols introduced in medical genetics during the candidate gene association study reproducibility crisis, where rigorous standards for statistical significance and correction for multiple testing were established.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C150 draw an analogy to medical genetics history, supported by appropriate citations (Ioannidis 2005, Hirschhorn and Daly 2005, etc.). The analogy is apt given the similar issues of multiple testing, publication bias, and need for rigorous standards, though the specific solutions differ between fields.

results.result: Sampling admixture graph space is useful for modeling population histories, but finding robust and accurate models is challenging because f-statistics are usually insufficient for identifying uniquely fitting models, necessitating incorporation of other evidence sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C154 summarize the main conclusions of the study, directly supported by the comprehensive re-analysis of published models showing non-uniqueness of well-fitting models. This is a well-supported inference from the data presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The limitations identified for complex admixture graph fitting do not invalidate other uses of f-statistics, including negative f3-statistics for detecting admixture, f4/D-statistics for testing population relationships, qpWave for testing ancestral population numbers, and qpAdm for estimating mixture proportions.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C165 appropriately clarify the scope of the study's concerns. These other methods remain valid because they either test specific hypotheses (C159-C161) or rely on empirical covariance matrices rather than specific deep history models (C162-C163). This is an important clarification supported by established knowledge and appropriate citations.

results.result: Most published studies have identified fitting admixture graphs through manual processes, and in nearly all cases many alternative models fit nominally or significantly better than published ones, suggesting strong claims should only be made when all well-fitting temporally plausible models share common features.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 represent the core findings and recommendations of the study. C2 is supported by literature review and citations. C3 is strongly supported by the systematic re-analysis data (Table 1, 19/22 cases). C4 is a reasonable recommendation based on the evidence, though it represents a normative conclusion rather than an empirical finding.
